system

Airport operations

An international airport of four terminals: who works with whom, every flight from slot to on-block, each bag from the drop to the hold, 120 stands, the turnaround at each of them, security, borders, de-icing and the desk that handles what goes wrong.

Levels12 machines · 17 flows · 11 systems · 2 mixedWritten byStatewright 0.2.1

  • 42levels
  • 97states
  • 134transitions
  • 6scenarios
  • 2findings

01 — Map

How the levels fit

Airport operations, the top level, as the Editor draws it; then every level, each a link to its part below.

Open full size

  1. Airport operationssystemFour terminals, two runways, 120 stands. The operations database is the source of truth for every flight; everything else listens to it or feeds it.
    1. Airfield surfacesystemEvery taxiway segment, holding point and stop bar the guidance system routes aircraft through.
    2. Operations databasesystemOne record per flight; adapters translate each partner's messages into it.
    3. Belt networksystemEvery belt of the four terminals. Bags flow left to right: drop, merge, screen, sort, make up.
    4. Bag lifecyclemachineIATA Resolution 753: every bag is tracked at acceptance, loading, transfer and arrival.
    5. Monthly billingflow
      1. Bill one operatorflow
    6. Boarding procedureflowFrom the boarding list to doors closed.
      1. Find the missingflow
      2. Board one passengerflow
      3. Offload the no-shows' bagsflow
        1. Offload one bagflow
    7. Border checkflow
      1. Secondary inspectionflow
    8. Check-in hallssystemCommon-use check-in: any airline at any desk, through the CUPPS platform.
      1. Terminal A hallsystem
      2. Terminal B hallsystem
      3. Terminal C hallsystem
      4. Terminal D hallsystem
    9. Cabin cleaningflow
    10. De-icingflow
    11. Emergency deskmixedThe airport emergency plan: alert levels, the call-out, and who comes.
    12. Flight lifecyclemachineA departure, from the published schedule to the hand-off to approach control.
      1. Climb outmachine
      2. Boarding phasesmachine
    13. Into-plane fuellingflow
    14. Disruption deskmixedA mixed level: a disruption's states, the steps the desk takes, and who it works with.
    15. Lost itemmachine
    16. Parking staymachine
    17. Flight alertsflow
    18. Passenger journeymachineWhere a departing passenger is, as the airport knows it — never who they are.
    19. Stands and gatessystem120 stands on five aprons. Contact stands are boarded through their gate; remote ones by bus.
      1. Gate boardingflow
        1. Board one groupflow
      2. Stand lifecyclemachine
    20. Screening hallssystem38 lanes in four halls. Each lane: divest, CT scanner, body scanner, recompose, and an alarm table.
      1. Security lanemachineOne of 38 lanes. A lane in alarm stops taking trays until the alarm is resolved.
        1. Alarm resolutionmachine
    21. Turnaround milestonesmachineEach region is one team's work on the stand; the turnaround ends when all six are done.
    22. Work ordermachine
  2. Notify passengersflow
  3. Turnaround procedureflow

Scenarios

A delay, then a new slot

Starts Thu 1 Oct 2026, 06:00

A delay while check-in is open; the network manager revises the slot and the flight goes on.

  1. StartStarts in scheduled.
  2. 1ctot.issuedscheduled → slot confirmed. Network manager sends ctot.issued.
  3. 2stand.allocatedslot confirmed → stand allocated. Airport operations centre sends stand.allocated.
  4. 3Until the next timerstand allocated → check-in open. Operations database receives Publish to displays. check-in opens falls due.
  5. 4flight.delayedcheck-in open → delayed. Operations database receives Notify passengers. check-in closes cancelled. Raises passenger.notified.
  6. 5ctot.reviseddelayed → slot confirmed. Network manager sends ctot.revised. Operations database receives Publish to displays.
A departure on time

Starts Thu 1 Oct 2026, 06:00

From the schedule to the hand-off, no ice, no delay.

  1. StartStarts in scheduled.
  2. 1ctot.issuedscheduled → slot confirmed. Network manager sends ctot.issued.
  3. 2stand.allocatedslot confirmed → stand allocated. Airport operations centre sends stand.allocated.
  4. 3Until the next timerstand allocated → check-in open. Operations database receives Publish to displays. check-in opens falls due.
  5. 4Until the next timercheck-in open → check-in closed. check-in closes falls due.
  6. 5boarding.startedcheck-in closed → boarding. Ground handler sends boarding.started.
  7. 6doors.closedboarding → doors closed → icing conditions? → ready for pushback. Cabin crew sends doors.closed.
  8. 7aircraft.offBlockready for pushback → pushed back. Air traffic control sends aircraft.offBlock.
  9. 8taxi.startedpushed back → taxiing out. Pilot in command sends taxi.started.
  10. 9aircraft.airbornetaxiing out → airborne. Air traffic control sends aircraft.airborne. taxi-out limit cancelled.
The airline cancels

Starts Thu 1 Oct 2026, 06:00

Cancelled after the stand was allocated: passengers told, stand released.

  1. StartStarts in scheduled.
  2. 1ctot.issuedscheduled → slot confirmed. Network manager sends ctot.issued.
  3. 2stand.allocatedslot confirmed → stand allocated. Airport operations centre sends stand.allocated.
  4. 3flight.cancelledstand allocated → cancelled. Airline sends flight.cancelled. Operations database receives Notify passengers. Airport operations centre receives Release the stand. check-in opens cancelled. Raises passenger.notified. The run is done.

A stand's day

Starts Thu 1 Oct 2026, 06:00

Allocated, occupied, cleared, free again.

  1. StartStarts in free.
  2. 1stand.allocatedfree → planned.

04 — Findings

What analysis found

2 findings, the most severe first.

Medium 1

FindingDetailWhere
L1mediumWayfinding still polls the old displays feed

The FTP feed is polled every 60 s; gate changes reach the signs a minute late.

Source: audit

Old displays feed, Wayfinding

Low 1

FindingDetailWhere
B2lowNo-shows' bags wait two hours before they count as mishandled

A rush tag after two hours misses the next bank of departures.
